paper.title_en: Calibrating the sound horizon by cross-correlating gravitational waves and baryon acoustic oscillations
paper.abstract_en: The cosmic microwave background measures the angular scale of the sound horizon at last scattering with stunning precision. A higher Hubble constant therefore requires either new physics before recombination that shrinks the sound horizon, $r_{\rm d}$, or a modified late-time expansion history. Current measurements of $r_{\rm d}$ either assume the early-Universe physics or import the distance ladder, repackaging the Hubble tension as a discrepancy in $r_{\rm d}$. Here we show that cross-correlating gravitational-wave sources with baryon acoustic oscillations can calibrate $r_{\rm d}$ within each redshift shell, where gravitational waves provide absolute luminosity distances and baryon acoustic oscillations provide acoustic angle measurements. The calibration needs no electromagnetic counterparts or gravitational-wave population models and depends little on the late-Universe expansion history. A ten-year third-generation gravitational-wave catalogue can obtain a $ 1\sigma$ $r_{\rm d}$ constraint of $1.40\%$ with the completed Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument survey and $0.82\%$ with the Chinese Space Station Survey Telescope and Square Kilometre Array 21\,cm intensity maps. Such a measurement would give the baryon acoustic oscillation ruler an absolute scale, independent of early-Universe physics and the distance ladder, and determine whether the Hubble tension originates in the early or the late Universe.
